column4: on 15 September, not wishing to be attacked while debarking, Turner's force retired at 1500 to a point southeast of San Cristobal; 24 hours later it turned north; on 17 September Turner decided to proceed

At 1500, 15 September, his force retired to a point southeast of San Cristobal to await more favorable conditions. ... Twenty-four hours later the force turned north toward the east end of San Cristobal to be in position to land the 7th Marines on Guadalcanal on 18 September. ... As the Japanese did not attack, Admiral Turner decided on 17 September to proceed with the landing plans.
column14: Miller, ch. V, p. 122; three passages from the same paragraph, each quoted exactly. The text before the first says warships were shelling the Lunga area almost nightly and Japanese forces were reported at the Shortlands. The staff log (Dyer, row 403) records the withdrawal on the afternoon of 15 September. Read as page text, 2026-11-15.

column4: Turner planned no more than twelve hours unloading off Kukum, because the force had to clear Sealark Channel before nightfall to avoid enemy warships; anchored on the morning of 18 September, unloading by 0550 and without interruption until 1800
column5: He planned to spend no more than twelve hours unloading off Kukum as his force would have to clear Sealark Channel before nightfall to avoid enemy warships. ... The force anchored off Kukum on the morning of 18 September and by 0550 had begun unloading. As Japanese aircraft did not attack during the day, unloading operations proceeded without interruption until 1800.
column14: Miller, ch. V, pp. 122 and 123. The first sentence is a plan made before the landing; the second is what happened. Hough (ch. 6) has the force anchoring off Kukum early on 18 September and Turner's force leaving at 1800. Men, tanks, vehicles and rations were left on board (land_unit_facts 621). Read as page text, 2026-11-15.

column4: Betelgeuse and her one destroyer escort retired, completely unloaded, at 1500 on 26 September; Alhena, with one destroyer escort, entered Sealark Channel that morning
column5: During the same morning the Alhena, escorted by one destroyer, sailed into Sealark Channel to unload. The Betelgeuse and her escort retired, completely unloaded, at 1500.
column14: Miller, ch. V, p. 123. "The same morning" is 26 September (Betelgeuse anchored again at 0630 on the 26th, the sentence before). Neither destroyer is named. Betelgeuse had been unloading since 24 September (land_unit_facts 1162), so the ship was at Lunga for three days, retiring east by night, for one cargo. Read as page text, 2026-11-15.

column4: three destroyers and three mine layers escorted the transports; four cruisers and five destroyers under Rear Adm. Norman Scott covered their left flank
column5: Three destroyers and three mine layers escorted the transports, while four cruisers and five destroyers under Rear Adm. Norman Scott covered their left flank.
column14: Miller, ch. VI, p. 142. Hough (the row after) has the same escort and cover. No ship is named. Read as page text, 2026-11-15.

column4: sailed under escort of three destroyers and three mine layers while four cruisers and five destroyers steamed off the convoy's left flank
column5: sailed under escort of three destroyers and three mine layers while a larger force of four cruisers and five destroyers steamed off the convoy's left flank
column14: Hough, ch. 7, p. 324. Hough names the cruisers in the next sentence. Read as page text, 2026-11-15.

column4: arrived off Lunga Point at 0547 on 13 October; interrupted twice during the day by bombing raids; the ships left completely unloaded before nightfall for Noumea with the 1st Raider Battalion
column5: arrived off Lunga Point to discharge troops and cargo at 0547, 13 October. ... Though interrupted twice during the day by Japanese bombing raids ... The McCawley and Zeilin, completely unloaded, embarked the 1st Raider Battalion and sailed out of Sealark Channel before nightfall to return to Noumea.
column14: Miller, ch. VI, pp. 142 and 143; three passages, each exact. The ships were off the beach from 0547 to before dark on 13 October. Read as page text, 2026-11-15.

column4: Sado, Azumasan, Kyushu, Nankai, Sakito and Sasako Maru, escorted by Akizuki and seven destroyers of Desdivs 2 and 27 under Rear Adm. Takama
column5: SADO MARU departs Shortlands for Tassafaronga, Guadalcanal, Solomons in a high-speed convoy also consisting of AZUMASAN, KYUSHU, NANKAI, SAKITO and SASAKO MARUs escorted by Rear Admiral Takama Tamotsu's [41] DesRon 4's AKIZUKI (F) and Desdivs 2's YUDACHI, HARUSAME, SAMIDARE, MURASAME and DesDiv 27's SHIGURE, SHIRATSUYU and ARIAKE.
column9: https://www.combinedfleet.com/SadoAA_t.htm (Sado Maru tabular record of movement, entry for 1942-10-13)
column14: combinedfleet.com, Sado Maru tabular record, entry for 13 October 1942 ("First Assault Convoy for Tassafaronga"); "[41]" and "[1]" in the page are its footnote marks. Six transports and eight destroyers by this source; Miller (row 417) says five transports and eleven escorting warships, with a footnote citing a source that says six ships were unloading. Not reconciled. Read as page text, 2026-11-15.

column5: The convoy carries about 4,500 troops including the IJA's 16th Regiment, two battalions of the 230th Infantry Regiment and 824 men of the No. 4 Maizuru Special Naval Landing Force ( SNLF) from Rabaul and Shortlands.
column9: https://www.combinedfleet.com/SadoAA_t.htm (Sado Maru tabular record of movement, entry for 1942-10-13)
column14: combinedfleet.com, Sado Maru record, 13 October 1942. The next sentence of the page lists a battery of 100-mm guns, a battery of 150-mm howitzers, a battalion of AA guns, the 1st Independent Tank Company, ammunition and provisions. Read as page text, 2026-11-15.

column4: air cover by the 11th Air Fleet and the R-Area floatplane fighters; the convoy arrived at Tassafaronga at midnight and began unloading; on 14 October carrier fighters from Hiyo and Junyo and R-Area floatplane fighters covered the unloading
column5: Air cover is provided by the 11th Air Fleet and the R-Area Air Force's floatplane fighters. At midnight, the convoy arrives at Tassafaronga and proceeds with unloading. ... At dawn, Mitsubishi A6M "Zeke" fighters from carriers HIYO and JUNYO and floatplane fighters of the R-Area Air Force provide cover over the unloading operation.
column9: https://www.combinedfleet.com/SadoAA_t.htm (Sado Maru tabular record of movement, entry for 1942-10-13)
column14: combinedfleet.com, Sado Maru record, entries for 13 and 14 October 1942. "At midnight" is entered under 13 October; whether it is the midnight at the start or the end of the 13th is not stated (the later events are dated 14 October). Read as page text, 2026-11-15.

column4: 14 October: Sasako Maru fired, beached and lost, her troops, tanks and guns landed; Azumasan and Kyushu Maru bombed and beached; troops, tanks and guns landed but the tank fuel and ammunition lost; Sado and Sakito Maru left Tassafaronga with their escorts at 1742
column5: She is beached and becomes a total loss, but her troops, tanks, and guns are landed successfully. ... The transports' troops, tanks, and guns are landed successfully, but the tank fuel and ammunition they carried are lost. ... At 1742, SADO and SAKITO MARUs and their escorts depart Tassafaronga for Rabaul.
column9: https://www.combinedfleet.com/SadoAA_t.htm (Sado Maru tabular record of movement, entry for 1942-10-14)
column14: combinedfleet.com, Sado Maru record, 14 October 1942; three passages, each exact (apostrophes as printed). The record says the convoy was attacked about 1030 by 25 aircraft from Henderson Field, about 1150 by B-17s and about 1330 again, and was attacked at 1740 by four SBDs after returning to Tassafaronga at 1700. From midnight to 1742 is the time the ships were off Tassafaronga by this source; no source read gives it as a figure. Read as page text, 2026-11-15.

column4: at dawn on 15 October five Japanese transports and their eleven escorting warships lay at Tassafaronga, ten miles from Lunga Point, unloading
column5: When day broke on 15 October, five Japanese transports and their eleven escorting warships were plainly visible from Lunga Point as they lay ten miles away at Tassafaronga unloading troops, weapons, supplies, and ammunition.
column14: Miller, ch. VI, p. 151; footnote 47 to this sentence cites the Strategic Bombing Survey as saying six ships were unloading. Miller dates the unloading to the morning of 15 October, combinedfleet.com to 13 and 14 October. Read as page text, 2026-11-15.

column4: the convoy landed all its troops, between 3,000 and 4,000 men, and 80 percent of its cargo
column5: succeeded in landing all the troops--between 3,000 and 4,000 men [footnote number omitted] --and 80 percent of their cargo.
column14: Miller, ch. VI, pp. 151 to 152 (the footnote number between the two parts is omitted from the quotation). The sentence before says air attacks seriously damaged the transports. Read as page text, 2026-11-15.

column4: the convoy left Shortland Harbor on 14 October; on 15 October around midnight the transports arrived off Tassafaronga Point; Sasako Maru was deliberately run aground, a total loss
column5: On October 14, 1942 departs Shortland Harbor and proceeds southeast down "The Slot" towards Guadalcanal ... On October 15, 1942 around midnight the transports arrive off Tassafaronga Point on Guadalcanal. ... Sasako Maru was hit by a bomb that caused a fire and was deliberately run aground but was a total loss.
column9: https://pacificwrecks.com/ship/maru/sasako.html (Pacific Wrecks Sasako Maru page, partial history and sinking history)
column14: Pacific Wrecks, Sasako Maru page. A tertiary page, one day later than combinedfleet.com (which has the departure and the midnight arrival on 13 October and the air attacks on 14 October); it gives the same escorts (Akizuki, Yudachi, Harusame, Samidare, Murasame, Shigure, Shiratsuyu, Ariake) and the same six transports. Kept as the alternative date. Read as page text, 2026-11-15.

column4: 12 October: the convoy left Shortlands for Tassafaronga but was recalled part way, and returned to Shortlands the same day
column5: Departs Shortlands for Tassafaronga but the convoy is recalled part way and steams back arriving at Shortlands later that same day.
column9: https://www.combinedfleet.com/SadoAA_t.htm (Sado Maru tabular record of movement, entry for 1942-10-12)
column14: combinedfleet.com, Sado Maru record. No reason, ordering officer or ships beyond Sado Maru are given. The page enters the line out of order (after 26 October), and it does not say what ships made this sailing. Pacific Wrecks (J14 rows) has the convoy leaving Rabaul on 12 October. Read as page text, 2026-11-15.

column4: search planes reported at about 2300 one Japanese transport and two destroyers in Sealark Channel; Scott attacked the larger force of cruisers and destroyers instead; the transport and the two destroyers escaped
column5: Search planes from the cruiser San Francisco also reported about 2300 that one Japanese transport and two destroyers were in Sealark Channel, but Scott decided to attack the larger force of cruisers and destroyers. The transport and the two destroyers escaped.
column14: Miller, ch. VI, p. 147, night of 11 to 12 October (Cape Esperance). Read as page text, 2026-11-15.

column4: at 2230 search planes reported one transport and two destroyers close inshore near Tassafaronga; they were ignored and departed the area at 0230 next morning
column5: At 2230, search planes reported one transport and two destroyers close inshore near Tassafaronga, but these craft were ignored and departed the area at 0230 the next morning.
column14: Zimmerman, ch. 6, night of 11 to 12 October. Gives 2230 where Miller gives about 2300, and Tassafaronga where Miller gives Sealark Channel. Read as page text, 2026-11-15.

column4: destroyer transports normally left the Shortland area, steamed southeast through the passage between New Georgia, Choiseul and Santa Isabel so as to reach the landing area at night; as many as 900 troops landed in a night at Cape Esperance; landings were generally accompanied by bombardment of the airfield
column5: At times as many as 900 troops were landed in a single night at Cape Esperance on the northwest tip of Guadalcanal by these ships which normally departed from the Shortland area and steamed southeast toward Guadalcanal, transiting the inside passage between New Georgia, Choiseul and Santa Isabel Islands so as to reach the landing area at night. ... Landings of this nature were generally accompanied by bombardment of the airfield by additional ships covering the landing
column14: USSBS, The Campaigns of the Pacific War, ch. VII, p. 115, on the destroyer transports that reinforced Guadalcanal from the Ichiki and Kawaguchi units onward. The first quotation is one sentence; the second begins the next sentence. A summary written from interrogations; times are loose. Read as page text, 2026-11-15.

column4: Lunga defenders could estimate 150 new enemy soldiers for every destroyer transport, often five or six a night, in early October
column5: Lunga defenders could estimate 150 new enemy ground soldiers for every destroyer transport--often five or six a night--that made the Express run
column14: Hough, ch. 7, p. 323, the American estimate at Lunga, not a Japanese record. 150 men a ship and five or six ships a night gives 750 to 900 a night, in line with the Strategic Bombing Survey's 900 a night (troop_lift_facts 26); no source states the sum. Read as page text, 2026-11-15.

column4: Japanese gunfire ships had to come late and leave early to avoid U.S. planes in daylight; Japanese ships still entered Guadalcanal waters nearly every night
column5: Japanese ships still entered Guadalcanal waters nearly every night, barges beached along the coast indicated many new landings ... Japanese gunfire ships had to come late and leave early to avoid the U.S. planes in daylight encounter
column14: Hough, ch. 6, p. 317; both quotations are in the account of 7 to 9 October. "Gunfire ships" are the bombardment ships, not transports. Read as page text, 2026-11-15.

column4: the Solomons waters changed hands every twelve hours: each side kept a trickle of aid going to its small force
column5: the Solomons waters changed hands every twelve hours, and thus each side kept an important trickle of aid going to its small combat force
column14: Hough, ch. 7, p. 322, October 1942. A description, not an order of either side. Read as page text, 2026-11-15.

column4: 21 September Kagero strafed by Henderson Field fighters while disembarking troops at Kamimbo Bay; three days later Kawakaze and Umikaze bombed and strafed there and both damaged
column5: On 21 September the destroyer Kagero was strafed by fighter planes from Henderson Field as she disembarked troops in the Kamimbo Bay area. Three days later, the destroyers Kawakaze and Umikaze were bombed and strafed at the same place, likewise by planes based on Henderson Field, and both were damaged.
column14: Zimmerman, ch. 6, p. 96. No man count. The same page says the rest of the 4th Infantry and all of the 29th Infantry had been landed by the end of September. Read as page text, 2026-11-15.

column4: 13 November 1730: Sado, Brisbane, Shinanogawa, Canberra, Nagara, Arizona, Nako, Hirokawa, Kinugawa, Yamaura and Yamatsuki Maru left Shortlands, escorted by eleven destroyers of Desron 2 (Hayashio, Amagiri, Kagero, Kawakaze, Makinami, Mochizuki, Naganami, Oyashio, Suzukaze, Takanami, Umikaze)
column5: in BRISBANE, SHINANOGAWA, CANBERRA, NAGARA, ARIZONA, NAKO, HIROKAWA, KINUGAWA, YAMAURA and YAMATSUKI MARUs escorted by Tanaka Raizo's (41) DesRon 2's HAYASHIO, AMAGIRI, KAGERO, KAWAKAZE, MAKINAMI, MOCHIZUKI, NAGANAMI, OYASHIO, SUZUKAZE, TAKANAMI and UMIKAZE.
column9: https://www.combinedfleet.com/SadoAA_t.htm (Sado Maru tabular record of movement, entry for 1942-11-13)
column14: combinedfleet.com, Sado Maru record, 13 November 1942 ("Second Assault Convoy for Tassafaronga"), the departure being "At 1730 ... from Shortlands" in the words before the quotation. Eleven transports and eleven destroyers by this page; Miller (ch. VII, p. 186) has eleven transports and cargo ships and twelve escorting destroyers (row 15); Hirokawa Maru's page (next row) lists the same eleven destroyers. Read as page text, 2026-11-15.

column4: the Reinforcement Unit in two groups: Group No. 1 Hirokawa, Nagara, Sado, Canberra and Nako Maru; Group No. 2 Brisbane, Shinanogawa, Arizona, Kinugawa, Yamaura and Yamatsuki Maru
column5: The Reinforcement Unit consists of two groups: Group No. 1 includes HIROKAWA, NAGARA, SADO, CANBERRA and NAKO MARUs while Group No. 2 includes BRISBANE, SHINANOGAWA, ARIZONA, KINUGAWA, YAMAURA and YAMATSUKI MARUs.
column9: https://www.combinedfleet.com/Hirokawa_t.htm (Hirokawa Maru tabular record of movement, entry for 1942-11-13)
column14: combinedfleet.com, Hirokawa Maru tabular record, 13 November 1942. Read as page text, 2026-11-15.

column4: air cover by the 11th Air Fleet and the R-Area floatplane fighters; on 14 November the "23-ship convoy" was sighted at 0849 by two reconnaissance SBDs
column5: Air cover is provided by the 11th Air Fleet and the R-Area Air Force's floatplane fighters. ... the 23-ship convoy is sighted by two reconnaissance SBD dive-bombers from USS ENTERPRISE (CV-6)
column9: https://www.combinedfleet.com/SadoAA_t.htm (Sado Maru tabular record of movement, entry for 1942-11-13)
column14: combinedfleet.com, Sado Maru record. The page counts 23 ships (eleven transports and eleven destroyers is 22; the page does not say which twenty-third). Read as page text, 2026-11-15.

column4: Kondo ordered the troop convoy beached at Tassafaronga; the four remaining transports were beached on 15 November; by dawn about 2,000 troops with 260 cases of ammunition and 1,500 bags of rice had made shore; most of their ammunition and food was lost
column5: Admiral Kondo orders Tanaka to beach his troop convoy at Tassafaronga. ... By dawn, about 2,000 troops with 260 cases of ammunition and 1,500 bags of rice made ashore. ... Most of their ammunition and food supplies are lost.
column9: https://combinedfleet.com/Yamatsuki_t.htm (Yamatsuki Maru tabular record of movement, entry for 1942-11-15)
column14: combinedfleet.com, Yamatsuki Maru record, 15 November 1942; three passages, each exact (the second is followed by the page's duplicated words "make shore"). Miller (the row after) has about 4,000 of the 10,000 troops landed and five of 10,000 tons of supplies; the figures are not the same measures and are not reconciled. Read as page text, 2026-11-15.

column4: of the convoy's 10,000 or more troops about 4,000 landed safely, without sufficient supplies and rations; only five tons of the 10,000 tons of supplies aboard were landed safely
column5: Of the ill-fated convoy's 10,000 or more troops, about 4,000 had landed safely on Guadalcanal, [footnote number omitted] but without sufficient supplies and rations. Only five tons of the 10,000 tons of supplies aboard the ships were landed safely.
column14: Miller, ch. VII, p. 188 (footnote number 44 omitted). Against combinedfleet.com's about 2,000 troops by dawn on 15 November (previous row). Read as page text, 2026-11-15.

column4: Turner's direct group sailed from Noumea at 1500 on 8 November, Scott's group left Espiritu Santo the next day and Callaghan's warships on 10 November; Scott's group arrived off Guadalcanal at 0530 on 11 November
column5: The ships under his direct command sailed from Noumea at 1500, 8 November. The next day Scott's group left Espiritu Santo; Callaghan's warships followed on 10 November. ... Scott's group arrived off Guadalcanal at 0530 on 11 November.
column14: Miller, ch. VII, p. 181. Scott's group carried supplies from Espiritu Santo and Callaghan's warships covered the movement (the sentences before). Read as page text, 2026-11-15.

column4: 11 November: Scott's group withdrew to Indispensable Strait at 1800; Zeilin, badly damaged, returned to Espiritu Santo with one destroyer as escort; the transports anchored off Lunga Point at 0530 on 12 November and, covered by the warships, began discharging
column5: At 1800 the group withdrew to Indispensable Strait. Damage to the Zeilin was found to be serious, and with one destroyer as escort she returned to Espiritu Santo. ... The transports anchored off Lunga Point at 0530, 12 November. Covered by the warships, they began discharging troops and cargo.
column14: Miller, ch. VII, pp. 181 and 182. Read as page text, 2026-11-15.

column4: 12 November: Turner, to avoid destruction by the enemy battleships, decided to withdraw all cargo ships and transports; they, escorted by destroyers, withdrew at 1815; Callaghan's and Scott's warships preceded them to Indispensable Strait, then returned to protect Guadalcanal
column5: To avoid destruction by the enemy battleships, he decided to withdraw all the cargo ships and transports. ... The cargo ships and transports, escorted by destroyers, withdrew at 1815, 12 November. ... Callaghan's and Scott's warships preceded them to Indispensable Strait, then reversed their course and returned to protect Guadalcanal.
column14: Miller, ch. VII, p. 183. The shares unloaded by ship are land_unit_facts 1166. Hours off the beach on 12 November, the transports having anchored at 0530 and re-anchored at 1525 after two hours stopped (land_unit_facts 1168), are not stated as a total. Read as page text, 2026-11-15.

column4: eight destroyers under Rear Adm. Tanaka in Naganami: 15th Division (Oyashio, Kurashio, Kagero), 24th (Kawakaze, Suzukaze), 13th (Takanami, Naganami, Makanami); no heavy ships, cruisers or transports
column5: Flagship Naganami (DD), Rear Admiral TANAKA, and the 2nd Destroyer Squadron which was composed of the 15th Destroyer Division ( Oyashio, Kurashio, Kagero ), the 24th Destroyer Division ( Kawakaze, Suzukaze ) and the 13th Destroyer Division ( Takanami, Naganami and the Makanami ).
column9: https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/AAF/USSBS/IJO/IJO-60.html (Interrogation Nav. No. 60 (USSBS No. 252), Capt. Toyama p. 254 (text after the --253-- marker))
column14: Toyama (chief of staff to Tanaka), USSBS interrogation 60, p. 254. Read as page text, 2026-11-15.

column4: left Buin on the night of the 29th; no air attacks going down or returning except flares during the night action; the troops and supplies were not landed that night, the ships returned to Buin, and they were landed later on 3, 7 and 10 December
column5: We had left BUIN on the night of the 29th ... No air attacks either going down or returning except flares which were dropped during the night action. ... No, we returned to BUIN. We landed the troops and supplies later on 3, 7 and 10 December.
column9: https://www.ibiblio.org/hyperwar/AAF/USSBS/IJO/IJO-60.html (Interrogation Nav. No. 60 (USSBS No. 252), Capt. Toyama p. 254 (text after the --253-- marker))
column14: Toyama, USSBS interrogation 60, p. 254; three answers on the same page, each exact (the third answers "Did you return and land your supplies?"). A recollection, three years after. JM-98 (row 183) has the first drum shipment begun on 30 November and the drums abandoned. Read as page text, 2026-11-15.

column4: the force moved toward Guadalcanal under cover of the shore-based reconnaissance aircraft of the 25th Air Flotilla, operating from Rabaul; two carrier groups covered it
column5: This entire force proceeded toward Guadalcanal under cover of the shore-based reconnaissance aircraft of the 25th Air Flotilla which, operating from Rabaul, searched as far as 164° east longitude.
column14: USSBS, The Campaigns of the Pacific War, ch. VII, p. 110, on the Occupation Force of 24 August. Zimmerman (ch. 4, p. 70) has the force screened by the light cruiser Jintsu and three destroyers and covered by two task forces each built around carriers (row 4 has four destroyers). Read as page text, 2026-11-15.

column4: four old destroyer transports (Patrol Boats 1, 2, 34 and 35) and Kinryu Maru, screened by light cruiser Jintsu and three destroyers, covered by two carrier task forces, the seaplane carrier Chitose closer in
column5: screened by light cruiser Jintsu and three destroyers. This force, in itself unable to cope with anything in the nature of an air attack, was covered by two task forces, each built around carriers
column14: Zimmerman, ch. 4, p. 70 (Patrol Boats named in the words before the quotation). The Strategic Bombing Survey has four destroyers (row 4); Toyama has four destroyers and four transports (row 6). Read as page text, 2026-11-15.

column4: Kinkaid's force (Enterprise, two battleships, two cruisers, eight destroyers) was to support Turner's force and all aircraft in the South Pacific were to cover the movement; Turner planned to land the 182d Infantry at Lunga Point and move the transports out of danger before the enemy could arrive
column5: Kinkaid's force at Noumea, consisting of the carrier Enterprise, two battleships, two cruisers, and eight destroyers, was to support Turner's force. In addition all aircraft in the South Pacific were to cover the movement of Turner's ships and to strike at any approaching Japanese vessels. ... He planned to land the 182d Infantry at Lunga Point and move the transports out of danger before the enemy could arrive.
column14: Miller, ch. VII, p. 181. A plan stated before the run, not a rule. Read as page text, 2026-11-15.
